marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Assess financial return from marketing investment.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (net return from marketing investment / cost of marketing investment) * 100
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Links marketing spend to profit accountability.
target_ranges: Positive and improving by campaign, segment, or channel
Compare against hurdle rate and alternative uses of capital
interpretation_notes: Include both short-term financial returns and long-term customer equity effects where possible.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Estimate net value of a customer over the future relationship.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: sum(expected contribution margin over time - service/retention costs), discounted to present value
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Guides acquisition bids, retention spend, and relationship tiers.
target_ranges: CLV should exceed CAC by a margin appropriate to business risk
Segment-specific targets are better than company averages
interpretation_notes: Assumptions about churn and margin drive results.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure cost to acquire a customer.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: sales and marketing acquisition cost / number of new customers acquired
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows whether acquisition is economically sustainable.
target_ranges: Should be materially lower than expected CLV
Track by segment and channel
interpretation_notes: Do not average together channels with different customer quality.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Compare customer value with acquisition cost.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: customer lifetime value / customer acquisition cost
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates whether growth spending creates value.
target_ranges: Often healthy when above 3:1 in subscription contexts, but category economics vary
Too high can signal underinvestment in growth
related_actions: Increase spend if payback is strong
interpretation_notes: Use segment-level ratios.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure how long it takes to recover acquisition cost.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: CAC / average monthly contribution margin per acquired customer
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Important for cash flow and growth pacing.
target_ranges: Shorter than cash runway and acceptable capital cycle
Benchmarks vary by category
interpretation_notes: A long payback may still be acceptable for durable, low-churn customers.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Track percentage of customers retained over a period.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (customers at end of period - new customers acquired during period) / customers at start of period
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Retention is a major driver of CLV and customer equity.
target_ranges: Improving over time
Segment-specific retention goals
interpretation_notes: Define active customer consistently.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Track percentage of customers lost over a period.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: lost customers during period / customers at start of period
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows leakage in the relationship system.
target_ranges: Lower is better; acceptable levels vary by industry and purchase cycle
interpretation_notes: Voluntary and involuntary churn should be separated.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure repeat buying among customers.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: customers with more than one purchase / total customers
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates whether value delivery leads to ongoing behavior.
target_ranges: Should rise as onboarding and satisfaction improve
Compare by cohort
interpretation_notes: Some categories have long purchase cycles.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure how often customers buy.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: number of purchases / number of active customers in period
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Drives revenue and share of customer.
target_ranges: Compare against category norms and customer need frequency
interpretation_notes: Do not push frequency beyond real customer need.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure average transaction size.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: revenue / number of orders
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Helps evaluate pricing, bundling, upsell, and product mix.
target_ranges: Improving without hurting conversion or retention
Segment-level tracking
interpretation_notes: AOV increases can hide declining customer count.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Estimate the portion of a customer’s category spending captured.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: brand purchases by customer / total category purchases by customer
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows growth opportunity within existing relationships.
target_ranges: Increase among satisfied customers
Track for high-value segments
interpretation_notes: Requires category purchase data or estimates.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Estimate total value of current and potential customers.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: sum of customer lifetime values across customer base
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Measures the customer base as a strategic asset.
target_ranges: Growing sustainably and profitably
Segment-level customer equity growth
interpretation_notes: Sensitive to CLV assumptions.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure whether target customers recognize or recall the brand.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: survey-based aided or unaided recall percentage
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Awareness is necessary for many purchase journeys.
target_ranges: Depends on category and stage; should improve among target segment
interpretation_notes: Awareness without relevance may not convert.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure percentage of target customers who would consider buying.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: survey respondents considering brand / target respondents
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Connects awareness to purchase probability.
target_ranges: Should rise after positioning and proof improvements
interpretation_notes: Consideration should be tracked against competitors.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure preference relative to alternatives.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: target customers preferring brand / target customers considering category
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates strength of positioning and differentiation.
target_ranges: Should be high in priority segments
interpretation_notes: May not equal purchase if availability or price blocks conversion.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Track composite strength of brand response.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: weighted index of awareness, associations, perceived quality, loyalty, and preference
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Captures brand asset strength beyond immediate sales.
target_ranges: Improving in target markets
Compare against competitors
interpretation_notes: Weights should match business model.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Estimate brand communication presence relative to competitors.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: brand media or conversation volume / category total
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Can influence awareness and market share when message quality is strong.
target_ranges: Appropriate to growth objective and competitive context
interpretation_notes: High share of voice with weak message can waste spend.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure sales position in category.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: company sales / total category sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows competitive performance.
target_ranges: Growing profitably in target segments
Compare volume and value share
interpretation_notes: Market share gains can be unprofitable if bought through discounts.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure category expansion or contraction.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (current market sales - prior market sales) / prior market sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Affects opportunity attractiveness and investment posture.
target_ranges: High growth can justify investment; low growth requires share or margin strategy
interpretation_notes: Use real market definition.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Track revenue growth over time.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (current sales - prior sales) / prior sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Core business outcome metric.
target_ranges: Positive and aligned with profit goals
Evaluate by segment, product, channel
interpretation_notes: Sales growth without margin or retention can be low quality.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure sales remaining after cost of goods sold.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: gross margin / net sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Determines ability to fund marketing, service, and profit.
target_ranges: Stable or improving unless strategy intentionally trades margin for growth
interpretation_notes: Track after discounts and returns.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure revenue left after variable costs.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: price per unit - variable cost per unit
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Key input for break-even, CAC, and CLV.
target_ranges: Positive and sufficient for fixed costs and acquisition economics
interpretation_notes: Average margin can hide product mix differences.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Find units needed to cover fixed costs.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: fixed costs / (price - variable cost per unit)
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Supports pricing and launch feasibility.
target_ranges: Achievable under realistic demand assumptions
related_actions: Adjust price, reduce cost, reduce fixed spend
interpretation_notes: Does not prove demand exists.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure demand sensitivity to price.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Guides price changes and promotion strategy.
target_ranges: Inelastic demand supports price increases; elastic demand requires caution
interpretation_notes: Elasticity varies by segment, time, and competitive context.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure percentage who take desired action.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: conversions / visitors or leads
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows effectiveness of offer, messaging, channel, and friction reduction.
target_ranges: Improving by journey stage and source quality
interpretation_notes: High conversion from low-quality traffic may not improve profit.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure ad or message click response.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: clicks / impressions
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates initial relevance of creative and targeting.
target_ranges: Benchmarks vary by platform and format
interpretation_notes: CTR is not business value by itself.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure spending efficiency for lead generation.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: lead generation cost / number of leads
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Helps compare acquisition sources.
target_ranges: Evaluate with lead quality and conversion
interpretation_notes: Low CPL can be expensive if leads do not convert.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure conversion from lead to buyer.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: new customers / leads
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows quality of lead generation and sales process.
target_ranges: Improving by source and segment
interpretation_notes: Long sales cycles require cohort tracking.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure proportion of opportunities won.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: deals won / qualified opportunities
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Evaluates sales and value proposition effectiveness.
target_ranges: Higher in target-fit segments
Track by competitor and rep
interpretation_notes: Do not increase win rate by avoiding ambitious opportunities only.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure time from qualified lead to close.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: average days between opportunity creation and closed outcome
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Affects cash flow and sales productivity.
target_ranges: Shorter when buyer risk is reduced and fit is strong
related_actions: Improve content, approvals, buying center mapping
interpretation_notes: Complex B2B cycles may be naturally long.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Estimate speed of revenue generation in pipeline.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (qualified opportunities * win rate * average deal value) / sales cycle length
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Combines pipeline size, quality, value, and speed.
target_ranges: Improving without lowering deal quality
related_actions: Increase qualified opportunities, win rate, deal value, or reduce cycle
interpretation_notes: Inputs must be consistently defined.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure revenue return on advertising spend.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: revenue attributed to ads / advertising spend
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Useful for paid media optimization.
target_ranges: Above channel profitability threshold after margin
Compare incremental ROAS where possible
interpretation_notes: Revenue ROAS ignores margin and incrementality.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure number of unique people exposed.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: unique individuals reached by a campaign or channel
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Important for awareness and launch objectives.
target_ranges: Sufficient coverage of target segment
related_actions: Increase media budget, broaden channels, improve targeting
interpretation_notes: Reach without frequency or relevance may underperform.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure average exposures per reached person.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: total impressions / reach
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Affects memory and wearout.
target_ranges: Enough for recall without causing fatigue
related_actions: Adjust media scheduling and creative rotation
interpretation_notes: Optimal frequency varies by category and objective.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure active interaction with content or brand.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: engagement actions / impressions or followers
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates relevance and participation.
target_ranges: Compare within platform and content type
interpretation_notes: Engagement can be vanity if not connected to journey outcomes.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure tone of online brand conversations.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: positive/negative/neutral mentions or sentiment score
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Signals brand perception and issues.
target_ranges: Positive and improving in target communities
interpretation_notes: Automated sentiment can misread context.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Gauge likelihood of recommendation.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: % promoters - % detractors or survey-based recommendation intent
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates potential word of mouth and loyalty.
target_ranges: Improving by segment and touchpoint
interpretation_notes: Use with actual referral behavior when possible.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure satisfaction with product, service, or experience.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: average satisfaction rating or % satisfied
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Predicts repeat purchase and retention.
target_ranges: High and stable in priority segments
interpretation_notes: Satisfaction does not always equal loyalty.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure complaints relative to customers or transactions.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: complaints / transactions or active customers
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Early warning of value delivery failures.
target_ranges: Low and declining; contextualize with complaint accessibility
interpretation_notes: Very low complaints may mean customers find it hard to complain.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure speed of initial support response.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: time from customer inquiry to first response
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Affects service satisfaction and recovery.
target_ranges: As fast as customer expectations and category norms require
interpretation_notes: Fast response without resolution is insufficient.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure time to solve customer issues.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: time from issue creation to resolution
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Key to service recovery and retention.
target_ranges: Shorter for high-severity and high-value customers
interpretation_notes: Quality of resolution matters.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure availability in relevant outlets or channels.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: outlets carrying product / relevant outlets
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows whether customers can buy where expected.
target_ranges: High for convenience goods; selective for premium/specialty goods
interpretation_notes: More coverage is not always better for brand control.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure percentage of outlets carrying the product.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: number of carrying outlets / total relevant outlets
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Useful for retail availability.
target_ranges: Target depends on distribution intensity strategy
interpretation_notes: Does not account for outlet size.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure coverage weighted by outlet sales importance.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: category sales volume of carrying outlets / total category sales volume
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Better reflects availability where customers actually buy.
target_ranges: High in priority outlets
interpretation_notes: Requires reliable category outlet data.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure unavailability at point of purchase.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: stockout incidents / product-location checks
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Stockouts waste demand and damage experience.
target_ranges: As low as economically feasible
interpretation_notes: Overcorrecting can create excess inventory.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure logistics reliability.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: orders delivered on or before promised date / total orders
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Distribution performance shapes satisfaction.
target_ranges: High and aligned with promise
related_actions: Improve logistics, inventory placement, carrier management
interpretation_notes: Promise dates must match capacity.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure products returned after purchase.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: returned units or orders / sold units or orders
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Signals product fit, expectation mismatch, or quality issues.
target_ranges: Low relative to category, or intentionally managed for trial categories
related_actions: Improve product information, quality, sizing, onboarding
interpretation_notes: Some returns can be strategic in online retail.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure percentage of target market trying the product.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: number of triers / target market or reached audience
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Critical for new product adoption.
target_ranges: Rising after launch and promotions
interpretation_notes: Trial without repeat may indicate weak product value.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure conversion from trial or awareness to regular use.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: new adopters / eligible target customers or triers
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows whether an innovation becomes accepted.
target_ranges: Improves as barriers are removed
related_actions: Simplify onboarding, reduce risk, communicate advantage
interpretation_notes: Define adoption behavior clearly.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure sales from recent products.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: sales from products launched within defined period / total sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates innovation contribution.
target_ranges: Category-specific; should match innovation strategy
interpretation_notes: Can encourage too many weak launches if misused.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure new product sales taken from existing products.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: lost sales from existing products attributable to new product / new product sales
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Protects total portfolio profitability.
target_ranges: Acceptable when new product improves margin, retention, or strategic position
related_actions: Adjust positioning, target new segments, manage line
interpretation_notes: Hard to estimate without tests or controls.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure usage of coupon or promotional offer.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: redemptions / offers distributed
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows promotional activation.
target_ranges: High enough to drive objective without over-subsidizing existing demand
interpretation_notes: High redemption can be unprofitable if mostly existing buyers.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure actual spending versus plan.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: (actual spend - budgeted spend) / budgeted spend
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Supports control and accountability.
target_ranges: Within planned tolerance or explained by approved reallocations
interpretation_notes: Variance can be positive or negative depending on opportunity.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure demand-side interest captured in search behavior.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: brand search volume / total category search volume or search impression share
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Useful digital proxy for brand interest and discoverability.
target_ranges: Improving relative to competitors in target markets
related_actions: SEO, content, brand building, paid search
interpretation_notes: Search data varies by platform and category.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure subject-line and sender relevance.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: opened emails / delivered emails
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Indicates initial attention in owned channels.
target_ranges: Benchmarks vary by list quality and category
related_actions: Improve segmentation, sender trust, subject line
interpretation_notes: Privacy changes can affect open tracking.

marketing_metrics_and_kpis.purpose: Measure content/action relevance among openers.
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.formula: clicks / opened emails
marketing_metrics_and_kpis.why_it_matters: Shows whether email content motivates action.
target_ranges: Improving by segment and offer
interpretation_notes: Use with downstream conversion.

decision_rules.rule_name: Reject non-actionable segmentation
then: Do not use it as a target-market basis.
Revise the segmentation around needs, behavior, or reachable value differences.
decision_rules.because: Segments must change decisions and be economically reachable.
second_order_effects: Better segmentation may reveal smaller but more profitable opportunities

decision_rules.rule_name: Prioritize segment fit over segment size
then: Do not make size the primary reason to target.
Score fit, profitability, competition, and access before committing.
decision_rules.because: Large markets can be structurally unattractive or expensive to serve.
second_order_effects: Resources shift toward customers the company can satisfy better

decision_rules.rule_name: Use concentrated targeting when resources are limited
decision_rules.situation: Startup or constrained business choosing market coverage
then: Select a concentrated or beachhead strategy.
Build deep relevance and proof before expansion.
decision_rules.because: Focused resources can create stronger customer value than diluted broad campaigns.
second_order_effects: Early traction creates reference value and learning

decision_rules.rule_name: Use differentiated targeting when segments justify complexity
decision_rules.situation: Multiple attractive segments with different needs
then: Develop separate offers or marketing mixes for selected segments.
decision_rules.because: Different customers may require distinct value propositions to buy and stay loyal.

decision_rules.rule_name: Avoid mass marketing in heterogeneous markets
then: Segment and target rather than using one generic offer.
decision_rules.because: Focused competitors can out-serve meaningful customer differences.
second_order_effects: More precise targeting may improve conversion and margins

decision_rules.rule_name: Add behavioral data to demographic segments
then: Layer in benefits sought, usage, loyalty, readiness, or occasion variables.
decision_rules.because: Demographics describe people but may not explain purchase behavior.
second_order_effects: More precise CRM and media actions

decision_rules.rule_name: Use socially responsible targeting for sensitive audiences
then: Apply an ethics review.
Avoid exploitative claims, manipulative urgency, and harmful offers.
decision_rules.because: Targeting power must be balanced with customer welfare and fairness.

decision_rules.rule_name: Select beachhead where pain and proof are strongest
then: Choose the segment with urgent pain, reachable buyers, short feedback cycles, and reference potential.
decision_rules.because: Early traction depends on focus and credible proof.
second_order_effects: Learning lowers risk for later expansion

decision_rules.rule_name: Do not position on an unimportant difference
then: Reject it as a core positioning claim.
Search for benefits customers value.
decision_rules.because: Differences create advantage only when customers care.

decision_rules.rule_name: Do not claim what operations cannot deliver
then: Delay or narrow the claim.
Fix delivery capabilities before communicating broadly.
decision_rules.because: Positioning must be delivered through the full marketing mix.
second_order_effects: Better internal alignment and service quality

decision_rules.rule_name: Use value proposition to align price and benefits
then: Check whether the price signal undermines quality perception.
Use price only if it supports intended value meaning.
decision_rules.because: Price communicates value as well as captures revenue.

decision_rules.rule_name: Reposition when perception no longer matches target value
decision_rules.situation: Brand performance stagnates despite market opportunity
then: Develop a repositioning strategy supported by product, service, channel, and communication changes.
decision_rules.because: Perception change requires credible proof, not only new advertising.
second_order_effects: Renewed relevance and new segment access

decision_rules.rule_name: Use positioning maps before entering crowded markets
then: Map competitor positions on dimensions customers use.
Seek a credible gap or superior value position.
decision_rules.because: Crowded markets punish undifferentiated offers.

decision_rules.rule_name: Design product from core benefit outward
then: Define core customer value first.
Then design actual and augmented product elements.
decision_rules.because: Customers buy benefits and solutions, not isolated features.
second_order_effects: Better fit between product and value proposition

decision_rules.rule_name: Use service evidence for intangible offers
then: Make quality tangible through people, process, physical evidence, reviews, guarantees, and demonstrations.
decision_rules.because: Customers need cues to evaluate intangible value and reduce risk.

decision_rules.rule_name: Shorten product line when complexity exceeds value
then: Prune weak items.
Clarify good-better-best or segment roles.
decision_rules.because: Excess variety can raise costs and confuse customers.

decision_rules.rule_name: Extend product line only with clear segment or price-tier role
then: Do not launch until target segment, price point, and cannibalization impact are defined.
decision_rules.because: Line extensions should expand profitable demand or defend strategy.

decision_rules.rule_name: Kill weak new product ideas early
then: Drop or archive the idea before major development spend.
decision_rules.because: Early screening prevents expensive commitment to poor ideas.

decision_rules.rule_name: Concept test before product development when uncertainty is high
then: Develop product concepts and test with target customers before building.
decision_rules.because: Concept testing reduces risk before product development investment.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use test marketing when launch risk is high
then: Run test marketing or controlled pilots.
Measure product, price, promotion, and channel response.
decision_rules.because: Testing under realistic conditions reveals problems before full rollout.

decision_rules.rule_name: Accelerate adoption by reducing complexity
then: Simplify onboarding, provide demos, offer trial, and make benefits visible.
decision_rules.because: Complexity slows adoption even when the product is superior.

decision_rules.rule_name: Modify mature products before harvesting
then: Consider market modification, product modification, or marketing mix modification.
decision_rules.because: Mature products may still grow through new users, usage occasions, features, or mix changes.

decision_rules.rule_name: Harvest or discontinue declining products when strategic role is weak
then: Reduce investment, harvest, divest, or discontinue.
decision_rules.because: Resources tied to weak products have opportunity costs.

decision_rules.rule_name: Do not price above perceived value
then: Lower price, increase perceived value, or change target segment.
decision_rules.because: Customers will not buy if price exceeds perceived value.
second_order_effects: Value improvement may support future premium

decision_rules.rule_name: Do not price below cost without strategic reason
then: Raise price, reduce costs, redesign offer, or discontinue.
decision_rules.because: Costs set the floor for sustainable pricing.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use value-based pricing when differentiated value is clear
then: Set price around customer willingness to pay and value delivered.
Use costs as floor, not the main starting point.
decision_rules.because: The firm should capture a fair share of the superior value it creates.
second_order_effects: Higher margins can fund service and innovation

decision_rules.rule_name: Use skimming when innovation is protected and premium segment exists
then: Launch with market-skimming price.
Plan later price steps for lower willingness-to-pay segments.
decision_rules.because: Skimming captures maximum revenue from early high-value segments.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use penetration when volume and price sensitivity matter
decision_rules.situation: Pricing new product for fast adoption
then: Launch with market-penetration price.
Manage path to long-run profitability.
decision_rules.because: Low initial price can quickly attract buyers and build share.
second_order_effects: Installed base can create future relationship value

decision_rules.rule_name: Use product bundle pricing to raise value and average spend
then: Offer a bundle at a price below separate purchase total but above contribution needs.
decision_rules.because: Bundles can increase perceived value and total profit.
risks: Margin leakage if discount too large
second_order_effects: Higher AOV and trial of additional items

decision_rules.rule_name: Use segmented pricing only when differences are legitimate
decision_rules.situation: Considering different prices for different customers or contexts
then: Implement segmented pricing with clear fences and transparent logic.
decision_rules.because: Different customers and situations can support different prices, but fairness and law matter.

decision_rules.rule_name: Avoid excessive promotional pricing for brand-building offers
then: Limit discounts and use value-added promotions instead.
Track reference price erosion.
decision_rules.because: Frequent discounts can train customers to wait and weaken perceived value.
second_order_effects: More disciplined promotion can strengthen long-term equity

decision_rules.rule_name: Use psychological price cues only when they support trust
then: Test price endings, reference prices, and tier architecture for perceived value.
Avoid deceptive reference prices.
decision_rules.because: Customers use price as information about quality and value.

decision_rules.rule_name: Respond to competitor price cuts by diagnosing motive first
then: Assess competitor objective, cost position, customer sensitivity, and value gap before reacting.
Choose hold, add value, lower price, or introduce fighter offer.
decision_rules.because: Automatic matching can trigger unnecessary price wars.
second_order_effects: Disciplined response protects profit and position

decision_rules.rule_name: Raise prices with value communication
decision_rules.situation: Costs rise or demand supports price increase
then: Communicate value, reasons, and options.
Consider smaller packs, tiers, or added service where appropriate.
decision_rules.because: Customers judge fairness and value when prices change.

decision_rules.rule_name: Never exploit crisis demand through gouging
decision_rules.situation: Supply shortage or crisis demand surge
then: Avoid price gouging.
Use fair allocation, transparent terms, and long-term relationship logic.
decision_rules.because: Short-term profit can cause long-term brand and societal damage.
second_order_effects: Trust can strengthen after fair treatment

decision_rules.rule_name: Use intensive distribution for convenience goods
then: Stock the product in as many relevant outlets as economically feasible.
decision_rules.because: Convenience goods lose sales when not readily available.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use selective distribution for shopping or premium-control needs
then: Use selective distribution with qualified partners.
decision_rules.because: Selective coverage balances access with service and brand control.
second_order_effects: Better customer experience and partner commitment

decision_rules.rule_name: Use exclusive distribution for specialty or luxury positioning
then: Grant limited or exclusive distribution where partners can deliver the brand experience.
decision_rules.because: Scarcity, expertise, and control can reinforce premium positioning.
second_order_effects: Stronger brand equity and channel commitment

decision_rules.rule_name: Add intermediaries when they create more value than they cost
then: Use intermediaries and define roles clearly.
decision_rules.because: Channel members can reduce customer search, place, time, and service gaps.

decision_rules.rule_name: Integrate channels when customers behave omnichannel
decision_rules.situation: Customers move between digital and physical channels
then: Build omni-channel processes, data integration, consistent pricing logic, and service handoffs.
decision_rules.because: Customers judge the total journey, not the internal channel structure.

decision_rules.rule_name: Resolve channel conflict before scaling channels
then: Clarify roles, territories, pricing, incentives, and service responsibilities.
Consider vertical marketing systems or partner agreements.
decision_rules.because: Unresolved conflict harms customer experience and partner motivation.

decision_rules.rule_name: Set logistics service level based on customer expectations and cost
then: Balance speed, reliability, inventory, and cost against target customer value.
decision_rules.because: Maximum service may not maximize profit if customers will not pay for it.

decision_rules.rule_name: Set communication objective before choosing media
then: Define target audience, desired response, and journey stage first.
decision_rules.because: Media choices should follow the communication problem.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use informative advertising for new categories or features
decision_rules.situation: Buyer awareness and understanding are low
then: Use informative advertising and educational content.
decision_rules.because: Customers must understand need and value before persuasion can work.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use persuasive advertising in competitive choice situations
decision_rules.situation: Customers understand category but choose among brands
then: Use persuasive claims, comparative proof where appropriate, and differentiation messages.
decision_rules.because: The task is to shift preference among alternatives.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use reminder advertising for mature, familiar brands
then: Use reminder and reinforcement communications to keep the brand salient.
decision_rules.because: Customers may need cues more than education.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use personal selling for complex, high-value, or B2B decisions
then: Invest in personal selling, consultative tools, and sales enablement.
decision_rules.because: Complex purchases require interaction, trust, and objection handling.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use sales promotion for short-term action, not weak value
then: Use promotion with clear objective, time limit, and profitability guardrails.
Do not use it to compensate for a bad value proposition.
decision_rules.because: Promotions can stimulate action but cannot create sustainable value alone.
second_order_effects: Trial or inventory movement when controlled

decision_rules.rule_name: Use influencer marketing only with audience-fit and authenticity
then: Proceed with clear disclosure, brand fit, and performance metrics.
decision_rules.because: Influencers work through trust and relevance.

decision_rules.rule_name: Avoid vanity metrics as primary digital success criteria
then: Add journey and business metrics such as conversion, retention, CAC, CLV, or brand lift.
decision_rules.because: Engagement alone may not create customer or company value.

decision_rules.rule_name: Respect privacy in personalization
decision_rules.situation: Using customer data for targeting or personalization
then: Use consent, transparency, data minimization, security, and value-adding personalization.
decision_rules.because: Trust is essential to digital engagement and customer relationships.

decision_rules.rule_name: Fix satisfaction before scaling acquisition
then: Prioritize product, service, onboarding, and recovery improvements before major acquisition spend.
decision_rules.because: Acquiring customers into a weak experience wastes spend and damages brand.
second_order_effects: Higher CLV and word of mouth

decision_rules.rule_name: Invest more in high-CLV customers
then: Provide stronger service, personalization, loyalty benefits, and account management.
decision_rules.because: High-value customers justify higher relationship investment.
risks: Perceived unfairness if service tiers are opaque

decision_rules.rule_name: Serve low-value customers efficiently and fairly
then: Use lower-cost service models and self-service while maintaining fairness.
decision_rules.because: Not all customers can be served with the same costly relationship level.
risks: Customer dissatisfaction if service is poor

decision_rules.rule_name: Trigger service recovery after complaint or negative signal
then: Respond quickly, diagnose, resolve, confirm satisfaction, and fix root cause.
decision_rules.because: Effective recovery can preserve loyalty and trust.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use loyalty programs to reinforce value, not bribe behavior
then: Create benefits that improve experience, recognition, convenience, or economics.
Track incremental retention and profit.
decision_rules.because: Loyalty rewards work best when they deepen real value.
risks: Rewarding purchases that would occur anyway
second_order_effects: Higher frequency and share of customer

decision_rules.rule_name: Use exploratory research when problem is unclear
then: Conduct exploratory research before surveys or experiments.
decision_rules.because: Poorly defined problems lead to wrong data and wrong decisions.
second_order_effects: Sharper hypotheses and better research design

decision_rules.rule_name: Use descriptive research to size and profile
then: Use surveys, panels, secondary data, or observation to estimate characteristics and behavior.
decision_rules.because: Descriptive research quantifies what is happening and who is involved.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use experiments for causal questions
decision_rules.situation: Need to know whether a tactic causes an outcome
then: Run controlled experiments or A/B tests where feasible.
decision_rules.because: Experiments isolate cause-and-effect better than observation alone.

decision_rules.rule_name: Start planning with market-oriented mission
then: Rewrite mission around customer needs and value served.
decision_rules.because: Products change; customer needs and value domains endure longer.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use objective-and-task budgeting when accountability matters
then: Build budget from objectives and tasks rather than percentage-of-sales habit.
decision_rules.because: Spending should be tied to what must be achieved.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use marketing dashboard only with action thresholds
then: Define owner, threshold, review cadence, and corrective action for each KPI.
decision_rules.because: Dashboards create value only when they trigger decisions.

decision_rules.rule_name: Reallocate from low-return channels after sufficient test
then: Reduce or stop spend and shift to higher-return or higher-learning alternatives.
decision_rules.because: Resource allocation should follow evidence and strategic role.

decision_rules.rule_name: Protect long-term metrics when optimizing short-term ROI
then: Rebalance metrics and budget to include brand equity, satisfaction, retention, and CLV.
decision_rules.because: Some marketing returns occur through future customer relationships.

decision_rules.rule_name: Market leaders should grow the category as well as defend share
then: Look for new users, new uses, and more usage while protecting current share.
decision_rules.because: Leaders often gain most from total market expansion.

decision_rules.rule_name: Challengers should attack weakness, not strength
then: Avoid frontal attack unless resources and advantage are sufficient.
Use flank, bypass, or focused attack on weaknesses.
decision_rules.because: Direct attacks against strong leaders are costly.
second_order_effects: Higher chance of efficient share gain

decision_rules.rule_name: Followers should avoid undifferentiated imitation
then: Follow market learning while preserving distinctive value and cost control.
decision_rules.because: Pure imitation invites comparison and margin pressure.

decision_rules.rule_name: Nicher should deepen specialization
then: Specialize by customer, geography, quality, service, channel, or product line.
decision_rules.because: Niches are defended by expertise and fit.
second_order_effects: Strong loyalty and reduced direct competition

decision_rules.rule_name: Use exporting when global uncertainty is high and commitment should be low
then: Start with exporting or indirect entry while learning the market.
decision_rules.because: Exporting limits resource commitment and risk.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use joint venture when local knowledge or access is critical
then: Consider joint venturing with aligned partners.
decision_rules.because: Local partners can provide market, legal, and distribution knowledge.

decision_rules.rule_name: Use direct investment when control and scale justify commitment
then: Consider direct investment after context analysis.
decision_rules.because: High control can support long-term strategy when opportunity justifies risk.

decision_rules.rule_name: Adapt global marketing when cultural or legal differences are material
then: Adapt product, promotion, price, or distribution while protecting core brand meaning.
decision_rules.because: Standardized programs can fail when customer and institutional contexts differ.

decision_rules.rule_name: Avoid sustainability claims without proof
then: Do not use the claim until evidence and operating practices support it.
decision_rules.because: Unsubstantiated claims damage trust and can be deceptive.
second_order_effects: Stronger credibility after proof is built

decision_rules.rule_name: Redesign harmful offerings before promoting them harder
decision_rules.situation: Social criticism or product harm risk
then: Redesign product, pricing, targeting, data use, or channel practices.
Do not rely on promotion to overcome legitimate harm.
decision_rules.because: Marketing should preserve long-run customer and societal well-being.

success_patterns.description: Growth comes from improving customer value before scaling demand generation.
prevention_methods: Measure value delivery before scaling acquisition
examples: Zoom-like simplicity and usefulness supporting adoption.

success_patterns.description: A firm wins by serving a chosen segment better than broad competitors.
prevention_methods: Monitor niche size and adjacent expansion
examples: Specialist B2B providers serving regulated industries.

success_patterns.description: The brand promise is reinforced by product, price, channel, service, and communication.
warning_signs: Customers repeat the same brand associations
examples: Luxury and specialty brands with tightly controlled experiences.

success_patterns.description: Research and analytics produce hypotheses that are tested and scaled.
examples: Digital marketers using A/B tests before national rollouts.

success_patterns.description: Retention, satisfaction, and advocacy compound the return on acquisition.
examples: Retail loyalty and subscription programs with strong onboarding.

success_patterns.description: Customers experience one connected journey across digital and physical channels.
examples: Beauty and retail brands blending stores, app, e-commerce, and loyalty.

success_patterns.description: A firm sustains premium price with superior differentiated value and proof.
examples: Apple-style skimming or luxury branding logic.

success_patterns.description: Responsible practices strengthen customer trust and brand resilience.
examples: Brands aligning DEI or sustainability claims with actions.

success_patterns.description: New product adoption improves when the company reduces complexity and risk.
examples: Freemium software or product sampling.

success_patterns.description: Resources shift toward high-potential opportunities and away from weak ones.
examples: Companies pruning weak lines to fund growth categories.

success_patterns.description: Employee enablement drives service value, loyalty, and profit.
effects: Customer loyalty and word of mouth
prevention_methods: Measure employee and customer metrics together
examples: Hotels and service firms with empowered frontline employees.

success_patterns.description: Customers participate because the brand creates identity, usefulness, or belonging.
examples: Brand communities in fitness, gaming, or lifestyle categories.

success_patterns.description: Distribution intensity matches buying behavior and positioning.
examples: Convenience goods intensive, luxury goods selective/exclusive.

success_patterns.description: Marketing and sales address each role in the buying center.
effects: Shorter sales cycles and stronger relationships
examples: Industrial suppliers and SaaS account teams.

success_patterns.description: Mature products regain growth through market, product, or mix modification.
examples: CPG brands launching flavors, formats, or occasions.

success_patterns.description: The company standardizes core brand elements while adapting to local context.
examples: Global retailers or platforms adapting pricing/payment/content.

success_patterns.description: Personalization increases value while respecting consent and privacy.
examples: E-commerce recommendations and lifecycle emails.

success_patterns.description: Each KPI has an owner, threshold, and corrective action.
examples: Marketing dashboards used in weekly growth meetings.

success_patterns.description: Marketing claims match operations, logistics, service, and finance.
examples: Same/next-day delivery brands coordinating marketing and operations.

success_patterns.description: Environmental or social constraints become product, packaging, sourcing, or model innovation.
examples: Brands reducing packaging or redesigning materials.

failure_patterns.description: The company increases promotion before proving the offer creates customer value.
prevention_methods: Validate value, satisfaction, and onboarding before scaling
examples: Paid acquisition into a leaky subscription product.

failure_patterns.description: The company refuses target tradeoffs and creates generic marketing.
examples: Small businesses using generic ads for all local residents.

failure_patterns.description: Segments are based on simplistic identity assumptions rather than needs and behavior.
prevention_methods: Combine demographics with behavior and qualitative insight
examples: Age-only generational campaigns.

failure_patterns.description: The advertised promise is not supported by operations.
prevention_methods: Use launch readiness and proof audits
examples: Fast delivery promise with unreliable logistics.

failure_patterns.description: Prices are set from costs without understanding perceived value or competitors.
examples: Premium product priced too low, signaling poor quality.

failure_patterns.description: Sales rely on frequent promotions that train customers to wait.
prevention_methods: Set promotion guardrails and add value-based offers
examples: Retailers with perpetual sale events.

failure_patterns.description: New channels undermine existing partners or create inconsistent prices and roles.
effects: Lost partner support and margin leakage
prevention_methods: Define channel roles and conflict resolution rules
examples: Direct e-commerce competing with retailers without policy.

failure_patterns.description: Channels operate as separate experiences.
examples: Retail customer cannot return online order in store.

failure_patterns.description: Research is performed but not tied to decisions.
prevention_methods: Start every project with decision and action thresholds
examples: Large surveys conducted after strategy is already set.

failure_patterns.description: Teams optimize likes, impressions, or clicks without business or customer outcomes.
prevention_methods: Tie metrics to journey and customer equity
examples: Social posts celebrated despite no conversion or brand lift.

failure_patterns.description: New product launch lacks trial, onboarding, or complexity reduction.
examples: Complex app launched without guided setup.

failure_patterns.description: A brand extension stretches meaning or credibility too far.
prevention_methods: Test fit and reason to believe
examples: A trusted food brand moving into unrelated electronics.

failure_patterns.description: Weak products remain funded because of sunk costs or internal politics.
examples: Mature lines crowding out new growth.

failure_patterns.description: The company matches every competitor cut without diagnosis.
warning_signs: Margins fall faster than share rises
prevention_methods: Assess competitor motive and customer value before reacting
examples: Retailer matching a temporary competitor clearance.

failure_patterns.description: The brand makes social or environmental claims unsupported by operations.
prevention_methods: Substantiate claims and change operations first
examples: Sustainability ads with unchanged packaging or sourcing.

failure_patterns.description: Personalization becomes invasive or unclear.
examples: Ads revealing sensitive inferred traits.

failure_patterns.description: Domestic marketing is exported without adapting to local context.
examples: Product size, payment, or message mismatch abroad.

failure_patterns.description: B2B sales focuses on one contact and ignores other roles.
effects: Long sales cycles and lost deals
prevention_methods: Map users, influencers, buyers, deciders, gatekeepers
examples: SaaS demo loved by users but blocked by IT/security.

failure_patterns.description: Complaints are handled slowly or defensively.
effects: Lost customers and bad word of mouth
prevention_methods: Empower response and fix root causes
examples: Airline or hotel complaint unresolved after multiple contacts.

failure_patterns.description: Marketing plan has objectives and actions but no measurement or corrective process.
warning_signs: No one knows what is working
examples: Annual plan not reviewed until year-end.

industry_applications.business_context: Local, service-heavy businesses with high repeat-purchase potential and strong location/occasion behavior.
recommended_actions: Segment by occasion: lunch convenience, family dinner, date night, delivery, catering.

Design service process for speed, friendliness, and recovery.
Bundle meals to raise average order value without eroding value perception.
common_mistakes: Discounting constantly instead of improving experience.
Targeting all diners with one message.

industry_applications.business_context: Experience-driven service businesses where satisfaction, reviews, and service consistency are central.
recommended_actions: Segment by trip purpose and value drivers.
Make intangible service quality visible through reviews, images, staff, and guarantees.
Empower frontline service recovery.
Use CRM to personalize repeat guest experience.
common_mistakes: Ignoring staff training as a marketing lever.

industry_applications.business_context: Attention-based market where discovery, identity, community, and advocacy shape demand.
recommended_actions: Build fan segments by genre, identity, platform behavior, and live-event propensity.
Use social platforms for storytelling and community, not only announcements.
Create staged releases to move awareness to advocacy.
Monetize through experiences, merch, memberships, and live events.
common_mistakes: Using one channel for all fan segments.

industry_applications.business_context: Digital-first selling with measurable journey stages, high channel choice, and retention economics.
recommended_actions: Segment by acquisition source, intent, category, frequency, and profitability.
Optimize product pages for perceived value and risk reduction.
Use lifecycle emails and personalization for repeat purchase.
Track CAC, CLV, AOV, retention, and contribution margin.

industry_applications.business_context: Physical/digital channel business where assortment, location, experience, and omni-channel integration matter.
recommended_actions: Define retail positioning before assortment and price decisions.
Integrate store, online, mobile, and social touchpoints.
Use merchandising, service, and events to create experience.
Track stockouts and weighted distribution.
common_mistakes: Assortment complexity without clear customer logic.

industry_applications.business_context: Subscription business where acquisition, activation, retention, expansion, and product experience drive customer equity.
recommended_actions: Choose a beachhead segment with urgent problem and reachable buyers.
Use freemium, trials, demos, or pilots to reduce adoption risk.
Map buying roles in B2B SaaS.
Invest in onboarding and customer success before scaling acquisition.
common_mistakes: Scaling paid acquisition with weak retention.
Selling to users while ignoring IT/security/procurement.

industry_applications.business_context: Geographically constrained business that wins through local relevance, trust, convenience, and reviews.
recommended_actions: Define trade area and high-value local occasions.
Claim and optimize local search and review profiles.
Use local partnerships and community engagement.
Build referral and repeat purchase programs.

industry_applications.business_context: Complex buying process with technical specifications, buying centers, long sales cycles, and relationship value.
recommended_actions: Map users, influencers, buyers, deciders, and gatekeepers.
Create technical, ROI, safety, and service proof.
Use consultative selling and performance review.
Build account-specific value propositions.

industry_applications.business_context: Trust-heavy category involving learners, parents, employers, institutions, or governments with outcomes and credibility concerns.
recommended_actions: Segment by learner goal, age/life stage, format preference, and payer.
Position around outcome, flexibility, support, or credibility.
Use trials, demos, testimonials, and transparent outcomes.
Design retention around progress and engagement.
common_mistakes: One curriculum message for all segments.

industry_applications.business_context: High-trust, high-risk decisions shaped by outcomes, access, privacy, and regulation.
recommended_actions: Reduce perceived risk with credentials, reviews, transparent processes, and patient education.
Segment by need state and access barriers.
Respect privacy in targeting and data use.
Coordinate appointment, service, follow-up, and recovery.

industry_applications.business_context: Trust, risk, regulation, and customer life stage shape acquisition and retention.
recommended_actions: Segment by financial need, life stage, risk profile, and relationship value.
Use transparent terms and education to reduce risk.
Avoid exploitative targeting.
Build long-term relationship and share of wallet.

industry_applications.business_context: Mission-driven organizations that must create stakeholder value, trust, behavior change, and sustainable funding.
recommended_actions: Define target publics and desired behavior.
Use clear mission-based positioning and proof of impact.
Design donor, volunteer, beneficiary, and advocate journeys separately.
Measure engagement and outcomes, not only awareness.

industry_applications.business_context: High-frequency retail categories where mental availability, physical availability, packaging, price packs, and promotions matter.
recommended_actions: Build distinctive brand assets and shelf visibility.
Use intensive distribution where appropriate.
Segment by occasion and benefits sought.
Manage promotions to avoid reference price erosion.

industry_applications.business_context: Premium positioning where exclusivity, symbolism, service, and brand heritage shape perceived value.
recommended_actions: Control distribution and service experience.
Avoid excessive discounting.
Communicate craftsmanship, heritage, identity, and exclusivity.
Use high-touch relationship management for valuable customers.

industry_applications.business_context: Digital adoption and engagement business with network effects, onboarding, experimentation, and retention challenges.
recommended_actions: Reduce onboarding complexity.
Use freemium or trial where it supports adoption.
Measure activation, engagement, retention, and referral loops.
Use experiments to improve value and reduce churn.

industry_applications.business_context: Style and identity category with rising scrutiny of sourcing, waste, pricing, and claims.
recommended_actions: Substantiate sustainability claims with sourcing and impact evidence.
Design products and packaging to reduce harm.
Segment by style, value, and sustainability motivation.
Balance accessible pricing with ethical cost structure.
common_mistakes: Claiming sustainability while encouraging disposable overconsumption.

glossary.definition: The process of engaging customers, creating value, and building relationships to capture value in return.
A state of felt deprivation.
The form a need takes as shaped by culture and individual personality.
A want backed by buying power.
A combination of products, services, information, experiences, or solutions offered to satisfy a need or want.
The customer’s evaluation of benefits versus costs relative to competing offers.
The extent to which perceived performance matches or exceeds expectations.
The act of obtaining a desired object from someone by offering something in return.
The set of actual and potential buyers of a product or service.
Building and maintaining profitable customer relationships by delivering superior value and satisfaction.
Direct and continuous customer involvement in brand conversations, experiences, advocacy, and community.
The total combined lifetime values of all customers.
The logic by which a company creates customer value and achieves profitable relationships.
Dividing a market into distinct groups with different needs, characteristics, or behaviors.
A set of buyers sharing needs or characteristics the company decides to serve.
Actually differentiating the offering to create superior customer value.
Arranging for an offering to occupy a clear, distinctive, desirable place in target customers’ minds.
The full positioning of a brand: the mix of benefits on which it is differentiated and positioned.
The set of controllable tactical marketing tools: product, price, place, and promotion.
Anything offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use, or consumption that might satisfy a want or need.
An intangible activity, benefit, or satisfaction offered for sale.
A name, term, sign, symbol, design, or combination that identifies and differentiates a seller’s goods or services.
The differential effect that knowing the brand has on customer response.
Positioning the brand on attributes, benefits, beliefs, and values.
Extending an existing brand name to new forms, colors, sizes, ingredients, or flavors in an existing category.
Extending an existing brand name to new or modified products in a new category.
A group of closely related products.
The set of all product lines and items a seller offers.
A model linking internal service quality to employee satisfaction, service value, customer satisfaction, loyalty, and profits.
The course of a product’s sales and profits over its lifetime.
PLC stage when a new product is first distributed and made available.
PLC stage in which sales start climbing quickly.
PLC stage in which sales growth slows or levels off.
PLC stage in which sales decline.
Developing original products, improvements, modifications, or new brands through the firm’s own efforts.
Systematic search for new product ideas.
Screening new product ideas to spot good ones and drop poor ones.
Testing new product concepts with target consumers.
Introducing a new product into the market.
The amount of money charged for a product or service, or values exchanged for benefits.
Setting price based on buyers’ perceptions of value.
Setting prices based on costs plus a fair return.
Setting prices based on competitors’ strategies, prices, costs, and offers.
Setting a high price for a new product to skim revenues from segments willing to pay most.
Setting a low initial price to attract buyers and gain large share quickly.
Setting price steps between products in a product line.
Pricing products required for use of a main product.
Combining several products and offering the bundle at a reduced price.
A straight reduction in price on purchases during a stated period or of larger quantities.
Selling a product at two or more prices where differences are not based on costs alone.
Pricing that considers the psychology of prices and not simply economics.
Prices buyers carry in their minds and refer to when evaluating a product.
Adjusting prices continually to meet characteristics and needs of individual customers and situations.
A set of interdependent organizations that help make a product or service available for use or consumption.
Network of company, suppliers, distributors, and customers that partner to improve performance of the whole system.
A channel with no intermediary levels.
A channel containing one or more intermediary levels.
Disagreement among channel members on goals, roles, and rewards.
Channel structure where producers, wholesalers, and retailers act as a unified system.
Channel arrangement where two or more companies at one level join to pursue an opportunity.
A distribution system in which one firm sets up two or more marketing channels to reach customer segments.
Stocking the product in as many outlets as possible.
Use of more than one but fewer than all intermediaries willing to carry the product.
Giving a limited number of dealers exclusive rights in territories.
Planning, implementing, and controlling physical flow of goods, services, and information.
Logistics concept emphasizing teamwork across company and channel organizations.
Activities involved in selling goods or services directly to final consumers for personal use.
Activities involved in selling goods and services to those buying for resale or business use.
Integrated marketing across in-store, online, mobile, and social channels.
Specific blend of promotion tools used to engage customers and communicate value.
Carefully integrating communication channels to deliver a clear, consistent, compelling message.
Paid form of nonpersonal presentation and promotion by an identified sponsor.
Building good relations with publics by obtaining favorable publicity, building image, and handling rumors or events.
Personal customer interactions by the sales force to make sales and build relationships.
Short-term incentives to encourage purchase or sale.
Engaging directly with targeted consumers and communities to obtain response and build relationships.
Creating and sharing useful brand content that engages customers.
Enlisting or creating influencers to spread positive brand information.
Using digital and social platforms for sales prospecting, engagement, and relationship building.
Net return from a marketing investment divided by the cost of the investment.
A meaningful set of marketing performance measures in a single display.
Measuring and evaluating results and taking corrective action to ensure objectives are achieved.
A document or operating plan covering analysis, objectives, strategy, actions, budgets, and controls.
A unit of the company with a separate mission and objectives that can be planned independently.
Portfolio-planning method evaluating SBUs by market growth and relative share.
Tool identifying growth through market penetration, market development, product development, or diversification.
Assessment of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
Actors and forces outside marketing that affect ability to build and maintain relationships.
Actors close to the company that affect its ability to serve customers.
Larger societal forces affecting the microenvironment.
Systematic design, collection, analysis, and reporting of data relevant to a marketing situation.
Fresh understandings of customers and the marketplace derived from marketing information.
Information that already exists somewhere, collected for another purpose.
Information collected for a specific research purpose.
Research used to gather preliminary information to define problems and suggest hypotheses.
Research used to describe market characteristics or functions.
Research used to test cause-and-effect relationships.
Huge and complex data sets generated by today’s information technologies.
Analysis tools and processes used to extract insight from marketing data.
Buying behavior of final consumers for personal consumption.
Need recognition, information search, alternative evaluation, purchase decision, and postpurchase behavior.
High-involvement buying with significant perceived brand differences.
Low-involvement buying with few perceived brand differences.
Low-involvement buying with significant perceived brand differences.
Mental process through which a person passes from first hearing about an innovation to final adoption.
Organizations that buy goods and services for use in producing other products or operations.
All people involved in the business buying decision process.
Purchasing through electronic connections between buyers and sellers.
Advantage over competitors gained by offering greater customer value.
Identifying and assessing competitors and selecting which to attack or avoid.
Firm with largest market share in an industry.
Runner-up firm fighting to increase market share.
Runner-up firm that wants to hold share without rocking the boat.
Firm serving small segments not pursued by other firms.
Marketing products and services within and across multiple countries.
Entering a foreign market by selling goods produced in the company’s home country.
Entering foreign markets by joining with foreign companies.
Entering foreign markets by developing foreign-based facilities or operations.
Socially and environmentally responsible marketing that meets present needs while preserving future well-being.
An organized movement to improve rights and power of buyers in relation to sellers.
Developing strategies and practices that create a world economy the planet can support indefinitely.
Marketing guided by principles of fairness, honesty, responsibility, transparency, and respect.
